Sample collection and preparation followed the detailed protocols published by Hohrenk et al. (2020) [24].', 'ProteoWizard_configuration_description': "ProteoWizard's msConvert tool was employed solely for format conversion—not for centroiding—to transform raw instrumental data files (Thermo *.raw format from the Q Exactive Orbitrap) into open, platform-independent profile mass spectra in *.mzXML format. No additional msConvert parameters or settings (e.g., centroiding algorithms, smoothing, peak picking, or filtering options) were applied during this step; the conversion preserved the original profile (continuous) data intact. The purpose was strictly to enable seamless import into Python (v3.9), R (v4.0.4), and Julia (v1.6.3) programming environments for subsequent custom centroiding processing.", 'process_procedure_description': 'The centroiding process consisted of five key stages: (1) Peak profile isolation—mass spectra were segmented into individual peak profiles using zero-intensity regions (naturally occurring in Orbitrap-MS data) as predefined boundaries; overlapping peaks were split at valley points, with each valley point assigned to both adjacent profiles; deconvolution was intentionally omitted to avoid computationally prohibitive non-linear regression on large HRMS datasets. (2) Log-linearized Gaussian regression—each isolated profile was fitted using Caruana’s linearization approach: the Gaussian intensity model Î(x) = Î₀·exp[−(x−x̂₀)²/(2σ̂²)] was log-transformed into a second-order polynomial ln(Î(x)) = β̂₀ + β̂₁x + β̂₂x², enabling efficient linear regression without iterative optimization. (3) Parameter estimation—the centroid position (x̂₀), peak width (σ̂), and height (Î₀) were derived analytically from regression coefficients: x̂₀ = −β̂₁/(2β̂₂), σ̂ = −1/√(2β̂₂), and Î₀ = exp[β̂₀ − β̂₁²/(4β̂₂)]. (4) Uncertainty quantification—standard errors of the parabolic fit (from linear regression) were propagated to compute uncertainties for x̂₀, σ̂, and Î₀, which feed into the Data Quality Score (DQS) calculation. (5) Output generation—centroided results (m/z–intensity pairs with associated uncertainties and DQS values) were exported to comma-separated value (*.csv) files. The algorithm is implemented natively in Python (v3.9), R (v4.0.4), and Julia (v1.6.3); third-party packages (listed in Supplementary Table S3) are auto-installed in the ready-to-use application. While the method supports both ESI-positive and ESI-negative modes and both MS1 and MS2 spectra, all examples and validation presented focus on MS1 spectra acquired in ESI-positive mode. The algorithm is chromatography-agnostic—peak spectra are treated as independent, enabling universal application regardless of prior chromatographic separation.'}
{'sample_description': 'The samples used in the research were grab samples collected from the effluent of a wastewater treatment plant located in Warburg, Germany (Stadtwerke Warburg GmbH). These non-target screening samples are characterized by a high organic load, which induces significant matrix-associated effects in high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS), such as signal overlay—making them particularly suitable for robustness testing of the newly developed centroiding algorithm. Sample collection and preparation followed the detailed protocols published by Hohrenk et al. (2020) [24].', 'msconvert_configuration_description': 'The instrumental raw data files—specifically Thermo *.raw files generated by the Q Exactive Orbitrap mass spectrometer—were converted to open-format profile mass spectra (*.mzXML) using ProteoWizard’s msConvert tool. Importantly, msConvert was used solely for format conversion and not for centroiding; no centroiding functionality or peak-picking algorithms were enabled during this step. The conversion preserved the full profile (non-centroided) nature of the spectra to retain all raw intensity and m/z point information required for subsequent regression-based centroiding. No additional parameters, filters, or preprocessing options (e.g., smoothing, deisotoping, or peak detection) were applied in msConvert, as explicitly stated in the text.', 'process_procedure_description': 'The centroiding process is implemented as a platform-independent, regression-based workflow available in Python (v3.9), R (v4.0.4), and Julia (v1.6.3), with third-party packages automatically installed via a ready-to-use application (details in Supplementary Table S3). The core procedure consists of five sequential steps: (1) Isolation of individual peak profiles from the profile mass spectrum by leveraging zero-intensity regions (in Orbitrap-MS) and valley-point splitting for overlapping peaks—where valley points are assigned to both adjacent profiles; deconvolution was deliberately excluded to avoid computationally intensive non-linear regression on large HRMS datasets. (2) Log-transformation of the Gaussian peak model (Î(x) = Î₀·exp[−(x−x̂₀)²/(2σ̂²)]) to enable efficient linear regression, following Caruana’s approach (1986) [26]. (3) Fitting a second-order polynomial (ln(Î(x)) = β̂₀ + β̂₁x + β̂₂x²) via linear regression to estimate parameters: x̂₀ = −β̂₁/(2β̂₂) (centroid m/z), σ̂ = −1/√(2β̂₂) (peak width), and Î₀ = exp[β̂₀ − β̂₁²/(4β̂₂)] (peak height). (4) Propagation of standard errors from the polynomial fit to compute uncertainties for x̂₀, σ̂, and Î₀, which feed into the Data Quality Score (DQS) calculation for Gaussian-shaped peaks. (5) Export of final centroided results (m/z–intensity pairs with associated uncertainties and DQS) to comma-separated value (*.csv) files. The algorithm operates independently of chromatographic context—i.e., it treats each mass spectrum as statistically independent—and supports both ESI-positive and ESI-negative modes, though all examples in the paper use MS1 spectra in ESI-positive mode. For TOF–MS data (e.g., from Samanipour et al., 2021 [23]), the same regression framework is extended using a Bi-Gaussian model instead of Gaussian, with implementation details provided in the supplementary material.'}

Key algorithmic components included: (i) Retention time prediction using Support Vector Regression (SVR) with a specialized string kernel—Paired Oligo Border Kernel (POBK)—trained on ~40 experimentally measured peptides with accurately annotated retention times acquired on the same instrument; the SVR model maps peptide sequence features (x_i ∈ X) to real-valued retention times (y_i ∈ Y ⊆ ℝ) for prediction on unseen sequences. (iii) Integer Linear Programming (ILP) formulation to globally optimize transition scheduling: the objective function maximized the number of scheduled transitions per experiment subject to constraints including maximum simultaneous transitions, instrument duty cycle, and coverage requirements across the target protein set; the ILP integrated predictions from retention time and proteotypicity models, along with optional external experimental evidence (e.g., from SRMAtlas), while explicitly accounting for prediction uncertainty to ensure robust protein coverage. AIPW combined (a) a propensity score model (logistic regression predicting statin use from all baseline covariates) and (b) an outcome regression model (linear regression for ICU LOS; logistic regression for binary mortality outcomes), yielding Potential Outcome Means (POMs) and ATEs. The analysis pipeline consisted of the following detailed steps: (1) Temporal alignment: All eye velocity and neural activity waveforms were aligned to saccade onset. (2) Residual generation: For each session, the mean radial velocity waveform and mean spike density waveform were subtracted from each individual trial’s waveform to yield residual velocity and residual neural activity traces—this step removed shared temporal structure that could induce spurious correlations. (3) Within-trial correlation analysis: For each trial, Pearson’s correlation coefficient was computed between residual velocity and residual neural activity waveforms across 201 discrete temporal delays (Δt), ranging from −100 ms to +100 ms in 1-ms increments; zero delay indicated perfect alignment at saccade onset; negative delays (e.g., −9 ms) indicated neural activity preceding velocity (termed efferent delay, ED). (4) Across-trials correlation analysis: For each time point t relative to saccade onset and each delay Δt, two vectors were constructed: (i) a vector of residual neural activity values at time t across all trials (length = number of trials), and (ii) a vector of residual velocity values at time t + Δt across the same trials; Pearson’s correlation was computed between these vectors. This was repeated for every time point in the saccade epoch (spanning typically −100 to +150 ms around saccade onset) and every 1-ms delay, yielding a 2D correlation map (time vs. delay) at 1-ms resolution. (5) Statistical validation: Significance was assessed via two shuffling procedures: (i) for within-trial analysis, residual velocity traces were randomly paired with residual neural activity traces from *different* trials within the same session (100 iterations); (ii) for across-trials analysis, elements of each residual vector were independently shuffled across trials (100 iterations). Unshuffled correlation coefficients exceeding ±2 standard deviations of the shuffled distribution were deemed significant (p < 0.05, two-tailed). (6) Duration quantification: For each neuron, the across-trials analysis was repeated on 100 shuffled datasets to compute a confidence threshold (mean ± 2 SD); the total duration of significant correlation was calculated as the sum of all time-delay combinations where the unshuffled correlation exceeded this threshold. (7) Laminar depth analysis: For the 145 neurons recorded with laminar probes (4–16 active channels/session), channel depth was used to assess depth-dependent effects; however, statistical analysis was limited by variable channel counts per session and insufficient per-channel trial numbers for robust layer-specific inference.'}

Prior to each block, participants performed three maximal voluntary contractions (MVC) using a homemade dynamometer; the highest value was retained to calibrate effort levels as percentages of MVC, enabling fatigue compensation (Zénon et al., 2015). For the effort-constrained task: after a 1000-ms fixation, participants viewed a reward (5/20/50 euro cents) for 2000 ms, followed by a variable-duration (500–1500 ms) fixation, then a gauge with a red target line indicating required force (12 logarithmically spaced levels from 0.34 to 15.22 × MVC); participants accepted or rejected within 6 s using 'Enter' (accept) or 'Ctrl' (reject) keys; upon acceptance, they squeezed the dynamometer until reaching the target level (no time limit), with real-time visual feedback showing integrated force (e.g., 25% MVC for 4 s = 50% MVC for 2 s), enabling trade-off between effort intensity and opportunity cost (faster trial completion increased total earnings). For the time-constrained task: participants viewed a reward amount (20 discrete values from 5 to 80 cents), then accepted/rejected within 6 s; upon acceptance, they squeezed for exactly 5 s, and final reward was proportional to gauge position at trial end (e.g., 50% height → 50% of offered amount); if the top was reached early (4 ± 5% of trials), integration continued but gauge remained fixed. The film was hydrated with phosphate buffer (prepared from NaHPO4 and Na2H2PO4 salts, POCH, Poland) in Milli-Q water (18 MΩ·cm), vortexed to form multilamellar vesicles, and extruded through polycarbonate filters with pore sizes of either 100 nm or 50 nm (Whatman, Germany) to generate homogeneous LUVs. Final lipid concentration was 50 μM. Liposome size distribution was characterized before and after each measurement using dynamic light scattering (DLS) on a NanoSizer ZS (Malvern, UK); average diameters were 120 ± 10 nm (100 nm filter) and 70 ± 10 nm (50 nm filter). Optical setup included pulsed diode lasers (LDH-P-C-470 at 470 nm and LDH-DC-635 at 635 nm, Picoquant) delivering 80 ps pulses at 40 MHz repetition rate; optical filtering comprised a 470/20 nm clean-up filter, a 505DRLP dichroic mirror, and a 510 nm long-pass filter (Omega Optical); excitation was focused via a water-immersion objective (1.2 NA, 40×, Olympus) with low laser power (5 μW at the back aperture) to minimize photobleaching and saturation. Fluorescence signals were autocorrelated using SymPhoTime software (PicoQuant), with adjacent τ values set to 16 for binning. For Monte Carlo simulations, 1000 independent region-of-interest images were generated per experimental condition by random sampling from a Poisson distribution using the pixelated Gaussian image model. Nonconvergent maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) fits were excluded from analysis. WM load (number of red circles) dynamically increased by one upon successful trial completion and decreased upon two consecutive failures; performance was quantified as the WM load of the last successfully completed trial. Distraction cost was calculated as the percentage difference in performance between distraction and no-distraction conditions. (2) Attentional Blink Task: A rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) of 14 images was displayed with inter-stimulus intervals (ISI) of 199 ms, 166 ms, 133 ms, or 99 ms across four consecutive levels, each comprising 10 trials (two per T2 lag 1–5). T1 appeared at serial positions 3–7; T2 followed at lags 1–5. Target categories (people, chairs, trees, flowers, llamas, fruit, birds) were randomized; non-targets avoided same-category repetition within 3 positions. After RSVP, participants selected T2 from four category-matched options. Trials ending with <40% accuracy at any level were terminated early. Proportion correct was computed per lag and ISI level; statistical significance was assessed using z-tests for proportions. (3) Selective Stop-Signal Task: Participants tapped both screen sides as two falling fruits passed through a response window (500–800 ms post-fall onset); 12 of 32 trials were selective stop trials where one fruit turned brown, requiring inhibition on only that side. A staircasing procedure adjusted the stop-signal delay (SSD) in 50-ms increments to maintain ~50% stop success; separate staircases were used for trials with vs. without advance cue (a glowing circle indicating which fruit might turn brown). SSRT was computed using the quantile method: Go reaction times were sorted in descending order; the RT at percentile equal to the participant’s overall p(stop) was identified, and the mean SSD for that trial type was subtracted to yield SSRT. Data from UIDs were concatenated, and participants lacking correct Go trials or with 0% or 100% stop success were excluded. (4) Decision-Making Task: Participants started with 500 points and made 30 choices between certain outcomes and lotteries presented on a circular spinner; 11 gain-only, 11 loss-only, and 8 mixed trials were randomly drawn from pools of 60 gain-only, 60 loss-only, and 30 mixed trials. Hypoxic postconditioning (HyP) was administered 10 min after TAO initiation: mice were placed in a calibrated hypoxic chamber where oxygen concentration was gradually reduced to 5% over 20 min, maintained at 5% O₂ for an additional 20 min, with relative humidity held at ~50% and continuous O₂ monitoring via calibrated sensor. The fibrosis quantification pipeline comprised six sequential steps: (1) cleaning of the slice (via background removal), (2) definition of the tissue border (by morphological erosion to exclude pleura), (3) identification of air ducts and their walls, (4) extraction of parenchymal region (excluding airways and pleura), (5) quantification of fibrosis within the parenchyma, and (6) assembly of tissue visualization. Module 2b (Particle filtering—manual)—interactive deletion of residual false-positive background objects in the binary mask (e.g., debris or staining artifacts) by user input; outputs included ROI mask, overlay, ROI file, measurements, summary, and count of remaining particles. Module 3 (Border definition)—morphological erosion (distance-based reduction) of the cleaned binary mask (output of Module 2b) to exclude the pleural layer; this step generated a refined parenchymal ROI excluding peripheral non-parenchymal tissue. {'sample_description': 'The soil samples were collected from Yuxi City (24.145°N, 102.476°E), Yunnan Province, China in 2019. Two adjacent loam fields—approximately 600 m apart—were selected: one chronically affected by black shank disease (caused by Phytophthora nicotianae) and used year-round for disease studies (disease group, D group), and the other serving as a healthy control field (healthy group, H group). A third treatment, the biocontrol group (B group), consisted of the diseased field treated with Bacillus velezensis S719 applied during tobacco seedling transplanting at a dosage of 210–330 g/km². The biocontrol agent was prepared by fermenting B. velezensis S719 in media at 29–31°C for 48 h at 150 rpm with 10% ventilation, supplemented with 0.2% sodium humate, followed by addition of 0.1% chitosan and 0.1% chitin. Tobacco variety used was Yunyan 99. Rhizosphere soil samples were collected during the peak disease period (~8 weeks post-transplantation, in July) using a zig-zag random sampling method; eight tobacco plants were pooled per replicate to form one rhizosphere soil sample. For each sample, the entire root system was excavated, vigorously shaken to remove loosely adhered soil, and the tightly bound rhizosphere soil (1–2 mm layer) was collected into self-sealing bags. Five biological replicates were obtained per treatment group (D, H, B). Samples were immediately frozen in the field and transported to the laboratory, where they were stored at −80°C until DNA extraction. Physical and chemical soil properties were measured but showed no statistically significant differences among groups.', 'KEGG_configuration_description': 'The materials and methods section does not mention or describe the use of KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes) database, software, pathway analysis, functional annotation, or any KEGG-related configuration, parameters, settings, or pipelines. DNA integrity was assessed via 1.0% (v/v) agarose gel electrophoresis, and concentration/quality were quantified using a Nanodrop One Spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, USA). PCR amplification was conducted with Phanta Max Master Mix Kit P515 (Vazyme, China) under a two-stage thermal cycling program: (i) initial denaturation at 95°C for 3 min; (ii) seven cycles of 95°C for 45 s, annealing at 65°C for 1 min (decreasing by 2°C per cycle), and extension at 72°C for 90 s; (iii) 30 cycles of 95°C for 15 s, 50°C for 30 s, and 72°C for 30 s; and (iv) final extension at 72°C for 5 min. Amplicons were verified by 1.0% (v/v) agarose gel electrophoresis and sent to Novogene Co., Ltd. for Illumina P300 platform sequencing. Raw reads were demultiplexed and quality-filtered using Vsearch (version 2.7.2) on the Galaxy platform (Afgan et al., 2018). Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs) were inferred using DADA2 (version 1.8; Callahan et al., 2016), and low-abundance ASVs (present in <5% of all samples or representing <0.1% of total sequence abundance) were removed, yielding 2,743 high-confidence bacterial and archaeal ASVs after excluding mitochondrial and chloroplast-derived sequences. Taxonomic assignment was performed using RDP Classifier (Wang et al., 2007) against the SILVA Small Subunit rRNA database (Release 138; www.arb-silva.de/documentation/release-138/) with a confidence threshold of 0.7 (Quast et al., 2012). Downstream microbiome analyses—including alpha/beta diversity, taxonomic composition, and differential abundance—were conducted using the MicrobiomeAnalyst online pipeline (Version 2.0), specifically its Marker Data Profiling (MDP) module (Dhariwal et al., 2017). Prior to analysis, all samples were rarefied to the lowest sequencing depth (48,602 read counts) to minimize sequencing depth bias. Alpha diversity was calculated using Chao1 and Shannon indices at both ASV and genus levels; beta diversity was computed using Bray–Curtis dissimilarity at ASV and genus levels. Taxonomic composition was summarized at phylum, class, and genus levels, with Proteobacteria-focused class- and genus-level relative abundance analysis (Figure 1); filtering criteria included minimum count = 2, prevalence >10% across samples, and merging of minor taxa with counts <10; only the top 15 most abundant taxa were reported. Differential taxa analysis employed hierarchical clustering heatmaps (Euclidean distance, Ward linkage algorithm) and LEfSe (Linear Discriminant Analysis Effect Size) to identify biomarker taxa distinguishing the B, D, and H groups.'}

Raw MS data files were converted to mascot generic format (MGF) for downstream processing. In MGF files, the x-axis represented the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) and the y-axis represented relative peak intensity. Spectral data were used to profile the urinary proteome per subject. Protein abundance was normalized as the ratio of the abundance of a given protein to the sum of abundances of all detected proteins in that individual sample. ELISA procedures strictly followed manufacturer instructions: samples were rapidly thawed at 37°C, immediately placed on ice to prevent complement activation, diluted, and loaded into microplate wells as quickly as possible. Urinary complement concentrations were normalized to urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio. Second, structural similarity matrices were constructed by converting SMILES strings into unique atom pair fingerprints (Chen and Reynolds, 2002) and computing pairwise Tanimoto similarities using the ChemmineR R package (Cao et al., 2008). Third, gene perturbation profile similarity matrices were generated separately for CMap and LINCS datasets: probe-level data were aggregated to gene level (for HGU133A), and for drugs with multiple experimental conditions, consensus profiles were derived using the Kruskal–Borda merging algorithm (Iorio et al., 2010); Spearman rank correlation was then computed between ranked gene perturbation signatures for each drug pair. First, inflammatory and CAD-associated genes were retrieved using PolySearch (a text-mining tool querying PubMed, OMIM, DrugBank, SwissProt, HMDB, HPRD, and GAD) with 'Disease-Gene/Protein Association' query type and 'Inflammation' keyword, yielding 589 genes prioritized by Z-score (>1 threshold), resulting in 78 genes; additionally, 68 inflammatory CAD-related genes were obtained from the CADgene database. Redundant symbols were removed to generate a non-redundant list of 124 seed genes (Table S1), of which 87 (70%) were functionally linked to CAD via FunDO-based disease ontology (DO) enrichment (e.g., atherosclerosis, heart failure, ischemia, cardiovascular disease). Second, a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was constructed using STRING 9.0 with high-confidence interaction score threshold of 0.7, incorporating experimental and predicted interactions from neighborhood, gene fusions, co-occurrence, co-expression, experiments, and literature mining. Third, topological analysis was performed in Cytoscape v2.8.3 using the Network Analyzer plugin to compute betweenness centrality (BC) and node degree; hub genes were defined as those with simultaneously high BC and high node degree, visualized with node size mapped to degree and node color (red-to-green gradient) mapped to BC values. Fourth, a regulatory network was built by promoter analysis using MatInspector (Genomatix software suite) to identify transcription factors (TFs) with ≥1 predicted binding site in the promoters of hub genes; TFs were grouped into families based on functional similarity, and the regulatory network was reconstructed in Cytoscape, focusing on TFs with high connectivity to target hub genes. Fifth, network robustness was validated via cross-validation: 97 test networks were generated by systematically deleting 1–4 hub genes—specifically, 22 single-node deletion networks (removing each of the top 22 highest-BC/degree nodes once) and 25 multi-node deletion networks (five iterations each for 2-, 3-, and 4-node deletions, where one hub gene was deterministically omitted and the remaining omissions were randomly selected from the top 22 nodes); hub retention accuracy was calculated as the proportion of the original five hub genes (IL-6, TNF, IL1B, VEGFA, PTGS2) retained across all 97 test networks. Sixth, functional enrichment analysis was conducted using ClueGO with right-sided hypergeometric statistical testing, Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction, and kappa score threshold of 0.3 to assess biological relevance of hub genes and their regulators in CAD. Finally, quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) was performed on peripheral blood or tissue samples from the 64 CAD patients and 64 matched controls to validate mRNA expression levels of the five hub genes and their common transcription factors identified in silico."}
